statement: A flag has 3 horizontal stripes. Each stripe is coloured with one of 5 colours, and two stripes that touch must have different colours. The top and bottom stripes may match. How many different flags are possible?

choices.misconception: I made all three stripes different colours, $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$, though the top and bottom stripes may match.
I let every stripe be any of the 5 colours and ignored the rule about touching stripes.
I remembered that the middle stripe must differ from the top one, but gave the bottom stripe all 5 colours: $5 \times 4 \times 5 = 100$.
I added the choices for the stripes, 5 + 4 + 4, instead of multiplying them.

hints: Colour the stripes from top to bottom.
Count the choices for each stripe in turn, given the stripe just above it. Each stripe only has to avoid one colour, and the choices multiply.
Top: 5 choices. Middle: anything except the top colour. Bottom: anything except the middle colour.

solutions.reliable: Colour from the top. The top stripe has 5 choices. The middle must differ from the top: 4 choices. The bottom must differ only from the middle (it may match the top): 4 choices. So there are $5 \times 4 \times 4 = 80$ flags. The transferable idea: when each choice only has to avoid its neighbour, count the choices in order and multiply.

whyOnTest: Tests the multiplication principle when each choice depends only on the one before it, without overcounting or overrestricting.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
